Question: What if you could give up one of your parent's skills without missing it, which skill would you give up and why?
Answer: I've relinquished most of my dad's skill sets, not because I found them of no particular use, but because I never had his aptitude for either heroics or mathematics. My father was a self-taught civil engineer who became a certified land surveyor in the state of Virginia, despite never attending college. He was also an avid hunter and fisherman who would go with friends to the North Carolina shore on occasion for Gulf Stream charters. The captain of the fishing boat my dad hired that day was a likeable enough fellow. He liked my dad. He liked my dad's buddies. He liked the case of Budweiser and handle of Jack Daniels Old #7 they brought along with them in a Coleman cooler. And as the sun set that evening, miles from landfall, it became apparent to my father and his crew that their captain had been sneaking refreshments throughout the day, when they found him sprawled out across the bunk in the boats cabin, snoring and unresponsive. Before my father took his second certification exam, he employed the services of the elderly woman who tutored me in grade school math, to help him brush up on his Polaris. Even back then, civil engineers rarely relied on the stars to orient themselves, but my dad wanted to prepare for all possible examination scenarios. As it turned out, he wasn't required to know Polaris to pass that particular test. But on the boat that night, miles from port, it was clear skies and moonless. He started the motor, engaged the prop, and aimed the prow straight towards Nags Head. I miss my father. I miss his calm and self assurance. I wish I was capable of taking an unfortunate situation and turning into an opportunity for the sort of simple heroics that he was capable of. I long to see the stars to guide me home.

Question: What is the process for administering medication to inmates in prisons?

I would get my furosemide in the morning and a lot of the guys were on BP medication — hazards of the lifestyle and all. But there wasn't a tongue check because nobody was going to squirrel away heart meds for bargaining later. We didn't have any cancer patients on our floor, but it was my understanding that, unless you were straight up dying, nobody got narcotics. Patient inmates would receive their meds in the sick bay itself, and if it was anything fungible, like benzos or opioids, staff would make damned sure those had been injected or digested well before their return to the pod. Most of us were experiencing withdrawal from some substance or other…me from alcohol and oxycontin…my cellmate from crystal meth and crack cocaine. Nobody ever received treatment for addiction. If you were in the mood for anything therapeutic, there was always prayer meeting.

Question: Can a handcuffed inmate be housed with unhandcuffed inmates?

Arm and leg restraints are only deployed when corrections staff are present and the prisoner is being transported from one place to another, attending court hearings, or being treated for a medical condition off-site. Unruly detainees within the facility can be kept in a restraint chair for up to two hours at a time, but if they remain a danger to staff and fellow inmates they will be placed in solitary confinement. Shackling is considered cruel and unusual punishment. Anyone who's spent any amount of time with their hands cuffed behind them in the back of a patrol car can tell you that this is a physically unsustainable position to remain in indefinitely. It's a legitimate form of torture. I was handcuffed upon my arrest, transport and booking, and during my post conviction processing. Otherwise — besides the concrete walls and armored doors of my cell and pod themselves — I can't recall ever being physically restrained during the serving of my sentence. I was free to pace the confines of my cage.

Question: What's the point of collecting Hot Wheels cars?

Question: If you lived in the South in the 1800s, do you think you'd support slavery?
Answer: My father's ancestors lived in Hematite Virginia during the mid-1800’s, an unincorporated community in the Allegheny Mountains which was sundered by the Civil War itself. When “the Restored Government of Virginia” based in Morgantown established the boundary that would eventually become the Virginia/West Virginia border in May 13, 1862, our family basically straddled a battle line. They lived in the Confederacy, but could cross over into Union territory by simply taking a Sunday afternoon stroll following church services. We have no record of which side their sympathies lay with at the time, but these were simple mountain folk. If they had any experience with slaves and slave owners at all, it would have been through the landed gentry with their boys and maidservants who visited the Sweet Chalybeate Springs to soak in the mineral baths and take the cure. To be disarmingly colloquial, “They had no dog in this fight.” And I doubt I would have either. Because as much as I may be tempted to romanticize about how progressive I would have been in the pre bellum land of my birth, I'd have been a product of my time just like everybody else back then. Nobody's gonna hop in their TARDIS and throttle the progeny of Klara and Alois Hitler in its crib. Nobody's gonna spirit John Brown away from his assignation with the gallows of Charles Town. Nobody ended up there because DOC was the be-all and end-all of their anticipated career in law enforcement. So — not to paint with too broad a brush — but stereotypically, you'd get your quieter, older guys who just wanted to get to the end of their shift with as little day room drama as possible, and your boastful and belligerent younger guys with a chip on their shoulder broader than a standard issue epaulet. Question: What is the maximum amount of time an inmate can serve in a county jail?

And most jails are overcrowded enough already without housing prisoners long term. But here in the USA with its many thousands of local jurisdictions, each with their various ordinances, economies and infrastructure, there are exceptions to any rule when it comes to incarceration. One of my podmates was doing a five year bid at the Salem/Roanoke County Jail in Southwestern Virginia. His lawyer had brokered a deal with the commonwealth’s attorney for him to avoid transfer upstate. He was a contractor with his own masonry business which he coordinated from our day room. During the week, one of his employees would collect him from the courthouse parking lot since he couldn't drive himself (habitual DUI) and shuttle him to the job site. This guy had multiple children by various partners and a thriving business in a small southern town. You send an inmate like that to Keen Mountain or Red Onion and it's a financial drain on the entire community. So that's why there's such a thing as work release. Sentencing judges have a great deal more latitude than one might assume when it comes to where a convict does their time. And the more responsibilities you have, the more likely your legal counsel is to take advantage of that fact. The law may not always be fair, but it can be remarkably flexible when it comes to the bottom line.

The only reasons I EVER removed my socks in county was — And that's it. Despite the CO’s wheeling in a janitorial cart once a day, and every con in the pod swabbing the day room floor, our individual cells (particularly the stainless steel toilet/sink combo), and the shower stall and additional open air communal head at the end of the second tier catwalk — despite all this — the surfaces in jail were never truly clean. It was early in my incarceration, and I was dealing with alcohol and opioid withdrawal as best I could in an environment where symptom mitigation was considered coddling. It was an uncomfortable read. And while Western romance and techno-thrillers may dominate the fiction selection in the male pods, true crime is the headliner in the nonfiction category. Exposés like Helter Skelter, In Cold Blood, and The Executioner’s Song — if they survive the facility's content censors — make for popular fare. But I was in a precarious psychic state myself, and in no condition emotionally to imagine living in some bucolic Scottish village, only to peer out my cottage window one evening to the sight of human viscera raining from the umber skies. …had to put it down, in fact. Inmates are rarely as tough as one might imagine. …in fact, are far more human than one might think.

Question: Do prisoners have the right to go on strike if they are not given enough food or good quality food while in prison?
Answer: In the United States of America, citizens lose three specific constitutional rights when they're imprisoned for a crime. And perhaps none of these is more controversial than that third suspension of rights, since the First Amendment is considered so fundamental to what it means to be an American. The administrators of federal and state prisons, as well as municipal jails, contend that allowing inmates to object to mistreatment, even though methods so benign as passive resistance, would interfere with their ability to maintain order. It could conceivably be helpful if the U.S. Constitution identified adequate nutrition and housing as basic human rights. But unlike most other representative democracies (as well as the United Nations), America doesn't recognize health and well-being as worthy of protection. If nothing else, our healthcare system should make that abundantly clear. Our Constitution was penned by a colonial gentry. …your basic bunch of wealthy landowners in powdered wigs and silk stockings. They didn't concern themselves with sustenance or shelter, because when you're the master of a Monticello or a Montpelier, edible food and affordable housing are the least of your worries. You want to keep your slaves in line and the octaroons underfoot to an easily ignorable minimum. Our judicial system is a relatively successful attempt to extend the institutions of chantel slavery and indentured servitude beyond their evident dilution in the 19th to early 20th Century. This is why men in chains harvest food to this very day in the fields of the Angola Slave Plantation, now the only maximum security state prison in the State of Louisiana, 161 years after Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation supposedly went into effect. And if you buy your food at Walmart or Target, then you are the beneficiary of this slave labor. I don't think it's too much to ask that prisoners be fed as well as the people whom benefit from the sweat of their brow. Seems only fair.

Question: Do inmates in the US prison/jail system keep their bedsheets when they move to another cell? If not, why?
Answer: You take everything with you which you were issued by the CO’s or purchased yourself through the commissary. You stuff your spare jumper, tube socks and underwear into a laundry duffel along with your linen (two sheets and a wool blanket) bath towel and wash rag. The yoga mat on your bunk comes off the welded metal pallet bolted to the wall to be replaced by the bedding of the cell's next occupant. Your commissary arrives once a week in brown paper grocery sacks. Those are helpful when relocating. Your toiletries can go into one of those, along with your chips, snack cakes and candy bars. When you get to your new cell, your bedding goes on your newly assigned bunk, while the bags go under it. If your new cellmate seems like a reasonable approximation of a human being, your tube of Colgate and bar of Ivory go on the edge of the stainless steel sink above the toilet. If he doesn't, you keep everything under your bed and guard it with your life. Nobody should have to share a roll-on deodorant and a toothbrush. Some cellmates can be clueless in that regard. Changes of address are always an adventure.

Question: Are prisoners allowed to have or grow beards in the USA?

And this is the reason why right here — That's a one-piece stamped stainless steel mirror with raised frame which is mounted to the wall just above your cell’s toilet/sink combo. Notice the blurry image of the cell window projected from its surface? That's roughly the quality of reflection you could expect when you peered into it trying to do detail work on some facial hair. It contains no glass, because that could be broken into shards and used as a weapon. But as reflective surfaces go, a burnished sheet of metal isn't optimal. Pair that with the dearth of edged tools in general, save for the occasional plastic disposable safety razor distributed and meticulously recollected by a corrections officer so nobody can squirrel one away for later…. And well…a beard can be more trouble than it's worth. So I suppose if you have THAT kind of relationship with your cellmate, then you could ask him to do your grooming for you, but I never really relished the notion of getting that up close and personal with my bunkie. There was a barber chair near the commissary where a trustee with a background in cosmetology and a set of Wahl clippers would trim you up for a fee. I never availed myself of those services, so I don't know if he did beards as well. There was a black barber on Wednesdays and a white barber on Thursdays. And that's the extent of racial profiling I encountered at the Salem/Roanoke County Jail.

Question: Can you sleep at night in jail?

The lights may dim, but they never go completely out, so unless you mask up, the florescent bulb over your stainless steel shaving mirror is going to shine in your eyes all night long. And I don't know how you feel personally, but I was never really comfortable wearing eye shades while incarcerated. Call me overly cautious, but I don't want to be fumbling with a blindfold when the shit goes down. CO’s make a particular point of creating as much noise as possible when they walk their respective rounds during graveyard shift. Deadbolts rattle. Armored doors slam. The hours rumble along like a gurney down a shuttered hallway. The pallets are hard and unforgiving. You take comfort while you can.

Question: Do all criminals fear going back to jail or prison? If so, why is this fear not utilized by society for our own benefit, such as through encouraging them to provide information (i.e. snitching)?

Question: Can an inmate choose to go to their cell early before the “lights out” call or do they have to go when the prison guard or warden tells them to?

I mean, you HAVE to make an appearance if you want to be issued a tray, and once you have it, you're required to sit at the day room tables to eat it. But if you don't mind missing a meal, you can simply answer when your name's called and go right back to napping or whatever. The pod's ceiling mounted TV can be remotely powered down from the floor’s control booth. When the screen winks off then you know it's time to vacate the day room and head for your cell…most nights at 11pm. …later if a ballgame runs long. 7am and it winks back on just before the tray trolley rolls in for breakfast. So, other than a toss, lockdown, or curfew, your movement between day room and cell remains unrestricted. It's pretty much the only freedom of movement you get in county. Don't let it go to your head.

Name: Robert Wade Bess
Question: What is the common fear of going to jail?

Like actual war as opposed to the cinematic variety, jail is — “…months of abject boredom punctuated by moments of sheer terror.” — WWI adage And once you're processed into the system, no amount of speculation on your part is going to be advantageous in the least. Your best strategy is to surrender yourself to its inevitability, like an overdose of cannabis edibles or a prostate exam. You make the best of it…might even enjoy it s bit if you're in the right headspace. So, by the time your time's up, you just might find yourself wondering what all the fuss was about. Which is, I suspect, why so many parolees eventually find their way on back inside. Because, while incarceration is meant to be a deterrent, its most likely lesson is that you can do that time standing on your head. Which makes it that much more likely you'll re-offend. The things we fear rarely end up being as bad as we imagine they might be. And in a way, that's a bit of a shame. I wish the threat of prison had been enough to keep me out of trouble.

Question: Did you suffer staying in jail or prison?
Answer: The alcohol and narcotics withdrawal was pretty bad for a couple of weeks, but after that, I was mostly just uncomfortable. We take for granted the misshapen and lumpy recliner, couch, or bed we lounge on to relax while watching TV, listening to music, or reading a book. But in jail, your choice is between the stainless steel stools in the day room — maybe some stackable plastic chairs — and the sheet metal slab that's the platform for the bed in your cell. …or you can crouch on the concrete floor in either location. And that's it. The “mattress" you get to sleep on is basically a sized down gym mat, and it's all that comes between your body and the cold hard surface of welded iron and rivets when you try to sleep. You get a couple of brown twin sheets and a wool comforter…perhaps a vinyl coated slab of cotton batting to lay your head on if you're lucky. If not, then your gym mat has a raised portion at one end that's supposed to suffice. We used to supplement this by using a laundry duffel stuffed with dirty socks and underwear for a pillow. I feel uncomfortable claiming that I suffered while I served my sentence, because in the grand scheme of things, it wasn't all that bad. But I don't think anybody's gonna be rehabilitated by being denied comfort and rest. And was anything really accomplished by making me and my fellow inmates as unsettled as possible while we rode our time out? Removal from society is supposed to be the punishment. Anything above and beyond that is needlessly punitive. (rest my case)

Answer: There's no surer way to destroy canned food than freezing it unopened. You're going to compromise the vacuum seal; might as well just throw it out instead. Plus, BEST BY dates aren't the death knell for unopened foodstuffs you imagine them to be. Question: Do prisoners discuss their pen pals to other prisoners?
Answer: An inmate in the cell next to mine was carrying out a correspondence with a girlfriend on the women's unit one floor below us. Understand, this wasn't supposed to be allowed, but the two lovebirds circumvented the facility’s prohibition against inmates’ writing each other by mailing their letters to friends on the outside who would forward them along. These missives were worthy of Penthouse Forum. I know this because my neighbor would offer up a public reading in the day room every time he got mail. I've given a lot of thought to the matter since my release, and I've come to the following conclusion: Despite the two being quite careful to never use each other's full names, there's still no way in hell the censors in the jail’s mailroom weren't aware of what was going on. I mean, this was straight up porn we're talking here…no pictures, granted…but still…bedside cabinet bottom drawer stuff. I think the CO’s were complicit. I think the screws were enjoying the free floor show as much as us prisoners ever did. It's hard to keep oneself entertained in lockup. The institutionalized monotony affect jailed and jailer alike. And much like the grub on the meal trays, the entire incarceration experience can benefit from a little spice. It's our dirty little secret.
